===== FILE 20834__1.pdf =====
Dr. Steven L. Lieberman​
Acting Under Secretary for Health U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs ​
810 Vermont Ave., NW ​
Washington, DC 20420 
Submitted Electronically 
September 3, 2025 
RE: 38 CFR Part 17 (RIN 2900-AS31), Proposed Rule, Reproductive Health 
Services 
Dear Dr. Steven Lieberman, Acting Under Secretary for Health: 
 
As Illinois’ statewide abortion fund, Chicago Abortion Fund (CAF) is in strong opposition to the 
proposed rule change that would:  
 
●​ reinstate an extreme abortion ban for anyone who gets their care from the VA with no 
exceptions for rape and incest or health of the pregnant person, and a narrow exception 
for life-endangerment, 
●​ restrict VA providers from providing information or resources about abortion care to 
veterans and their families, and 
●​ eliminate coverage of abortion care costs through the VA health program. 
 
As a body that is charged with a responsibility to provide care to “promote, preserve, or restore 
the health” of veterans and their families, this proposal is not only antithetical to the mission of 
the VA, but also particularly dangerous in light of a national reproductive healthcare crisis. Since 
the Dobbs v. Jackson Whole Woman’s Health Organization decision that overturned Roe v. 
Wade, the Chicago Abortion Fund has fielded over 45,000 support requests and distributed over 
$16 million to directly address barriers to abortion care. This is a testament to an already dire 
landscape for abortion access in the United States. By proposing an extreme abortion ban, 
alongside restrictions on information sharing and coverage, the VA is endangering veterans and 
their families even further. 
 
A.​ Abortion care is a necessary form of healthcare that improves family and health 
outcomes – and its availability fulfills the VA’s mission to “promote, preserve, or 
restore the health” of veterans and their families.  
 

 
 
When people are forced to remain pregnant against their will, they will have worse financial, 
health, and family outcomes. ANSIRH’s Turnaway Study, a longitudinal study that examines the 
effects of being denied an abortion on people's lives. Directly quoted from the study summary1, 
people who are denied wanted abortions are: 
 
●​ More likely to experience serious complications from the end of pregnancy including 
eclampsia and death. 
●​ More likely to stay tethered to abusive partners. 
●​ More likely to suffer anxiety and loss of self-esteem in the short term after being 
denied abortion. 
●​ Less likely to have aspirational life plans for the coming year. 
●​ More likely to experience poor physical health for years after the pregnancy, including 
chronic pain and gestational hypertension. 
●​ The study also finds that being denied abortion has serious implications for the 
children born of unwanted pregnancy, as well as for the existing children in the family. 
(Greene Foster et al., The Turnaway Study | ANSIRH 2020) 
 
Through this study it is clear that when people are denied access to the abortion care they want 
and need, their personal health and family outcomes worsen. The proposed rule change will 
push abortion out of reach for veterans and their families, and will negatively impact their health 
and wellbeing – a direct contradiction to the mission of the VA. 
 
B.​ This proposed rule change will cause veterans and their families to face 
heightened barriers to abortion care in the face of an already-present healthcare 
crisis. 
 
Since the Dobbs v. Jackson Whole Woman’s Health Organization decision in June 2022, the 
Chicago Abortion Fund has supported both veterans and family members of veterans, who were 
facing financial and/or logistical barriers to their abortion care. This has included:  
 
●​ A disabled veteran and single mother of two in a restrictive Midwest state who required 
an abortion at a hospital that would cost her over $3,000 without CAF’s support, 
●​ A mother from the South who needed a ride, flight, and hotel room to leave her state for 
an abortion – on top of over $700 in medical costs due to lack of insurance coverage, 
1 Greene Foster, D., Biggs, M. A., Gould, H., Kimport, K., Raifman, S., Ralph, L., Roberts, S., Rocha, C., 
Woodruff, K., Upadhyay, U., & Sisson, G. (2020). The Turnaway Study | ANSIRH. The Turnaway Study. 
https://www.ansirh.org/research/ongoing/turnaway-study  
 
 

 
●​ A Texan enrolled in VA insurance that was ending a wanted pregnancy after receiving 
news of a fetal anomaly, and who needed financial assistance in addition to emotional 
support resources, and 
●​ An overwhelmed veteran who was already a parent of two children with disabilities, and 
needed support with gas and appointment costs to make it to Illinois from the South. 
 
Without the support of the Chicago Abortion Fund, these veterans and family members of 
veterans would have faced even more extreme barriers to their abortion care – and some may 
have never received care at all. Since the VA benefits package has expanded to include 
abortions, an average of 140 people annually have received care through the agency. The 
above cases are a testament to the fact that the agency should be expanding its capacity to 
provide and educate beneficiaries on their options regarding abortion care, not restricting it 
completely. 
 
We know that the proposed rule would further exacerbate the devastating obstacles that people 
already face when they need an abortion, regardless of the reason they need care. In a moment 
when abortion care has lost its constitutional protections, this proposed rule will implement one 
of the most extreme abortion bans in the country. Without exceptions for rape, incest, or health 
of the pregnant person, this proposed ban has only one exception that uses the nebulous and 
historically dangerous language of only permitting care “when a physician certifies that the life of 
the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term.” We know that this type of 
narrow exception has resulted in delays to necessary healthcare, endangering the health, future 
fertility, and even life of pregnant people experiencing medical emergencies. 
 
This rule would not only force people to endure unnecessary hardship while attempting to 
access abortion care, but it would also force countless more to remain pregnant against their 
will and face worsened future health outcomes. CAF remains strongly opposed to this rule, in 
the name of the health, wellbeing, and futures of veterans and their families nationwide.  
 
Signed,  
​
Chicago Abortion Fund
